Authors: Liu, Y.; Li, B.; Yang, S.; Li, Z.
Source: Handling missing values and imbalanced classes in machine learning to predict consumer preference: Demonstrations and comparisons to prominent methods
Abstract: Consumer preference prediction aims to predict consumers’ future purchases based on their historical behavior-level data. Using machine learning algorithms, the prediction results provide evidence to conduct commercial activities and further improve consumer experiences. However, missing values and imbalanced class problems of consumer behavioral data always make machine learning algorithms ineffective. While several methods have been proposed to address missing data or imbalanced class problems, few works have considered the relationships among missing mechanisms, imputation algorithms, imbalanced class methods, and the effectiveness of classification algorithms that use impute data. In this study, we aim to propose an adaptive process for selecting the optimal combination of amputation, imputation, imbalance treatment, and classification based on classification performance. Our research extends the literature by showing significant interaction effects between 1) the amputation mechanism and imputation algorithms, 2) imputation and imbalance treatments, and 3) imbalance treatments and classification algorithms. Using three consumer behavioral datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, we empirically show that, among different classification methods, the overall performance of Random Forest is better than that of Logit, SVM, or Decision Tree. Moreover, Logit, as the most widely used classification method, suffers most from imbalance issues in real-world datasets. Furthermore, Metacost is always the best imbalance treatment for different imputation techniques or missing value mechanisms.
Methods: Empirical comparison study using three UCI consumer behavior datasets, 5-fold cross-validation, simulated missingness under MCAR/MAR/MNAR, MICE-based imputation (PMM, CART, Random Forest), imbalance treatments (down-sampling, bootstrapping, SMOTE, MetaCost), and four classifiers (Logit, Decision Tree, Random Forest, SVM).
Results: Random Forest outperformed Logit, SVM, and Decision Tree overall; MetaCost was the best imbalance treatment across imputations and missingness mechanisms. Imbalance treatment improved f-measure by 8.43% vs 0.01% for imputation alone, and MNAR performed slightly better than MAR or MCAR.
Conclusions: An adaptive pipeline considering missingness, imputation, imbalance treatment, and classifier choice improves consumer preference prediction, especially for imbalanced data. Limitations include testing only widely used algorithms, introducing missing values only in training data, and using three datasets.

Authors: de Almeida, F.G.; Baggström, A.; Andermann, T.
Source: Estimating national Red List statuses for fungi in Sweden - An improved deep learning approach to account for unbalanced data
Abstract: National and international extinction threat assessments provide critical data for research and conservation. Yet, many taxa remain unassessed due to the intensive data requirements of manual evaluations. For example, in Sweden, fewer than 40 % of known fungal species have an assigned extinction risk in the national Red List. To address this, approximation methods have emerged to provide estimates of extinction risk for species lacking an officially assigned status. These automated extinction threat inferences can be viewed as a best-evidence approximation, flagging potentially threatened species for further ecological research and targeted manual Red List assessments. One such approximation method is the deep learning approach implemented in the IUCNN package, predicting extinction risk using environment features extracted from species occurrence data. However, such approximation models face challenges arising from class imbalances, with most species classified as Least Concern, which biases predictions. Here, we advance the IUCNN framework by applying balanced accuracy as a performance metric and using class weights and oversampling to mitigate class imbalance. This approach improves the model's ability to predict intermediate classes, such as Near Threatened (NT), Vulnerable (VU), and Endangered (EN), resulting in higher overall balanced accuracy. We applied this approach nationally to 1445 unassessed Swedish fungal species, covering nearly half of the country's known fungi and increasing the number of fungi with a national extinction threat status by over 10 %. Our approach identified 661 species as potentially threatened, doubling the total of fungal species listed as threatened compared to the existing Swedish Red List assessments. This highlights previously unrecognized conservation priorities by shortlisting potentially threatened species that would be good targets to receive more attention from conservation authorities and manual Red List assessments.
Methods: National Red List prediction for 4611 Swedish fungal species using IUCNN neural networks in TensorFlow. The study compared baseline, class-weighted, and SMOTE oversampling models with 5-fold stratified cross-validation, balanced accuracy, and permutation feature importance.
Results: Balanced accuracy and oversampling performed best, with 0.41 balanced accuracy in the 5-class model and 0.76 in the binary model. The final model predicted 661 species as potentially threatened; tree height, biomass, and human population density were important predictors.
Conclusions: Accounting for class imbalance improved national Red List prediction, and the approach can flag previously unrecognized conservation priorities. A key limitation is that over half of Swedish fungal species lacked sufficient occurrence data for modeling.

Authors: Di Martino, F.; Delmastro, F.; Dolciotti, C.
Source: Explainable AI for malnutrition risk prediction from m-Health and clinical data
Abstract: Malnutrition is a serious and prevalent health problem in the older population, and especially in hospitalised or institutionalised subjects. Accurate and early risk detection is essential for malnutrition management and prevention. M-health services empowered with Artificial Intelligence (AI) may lead to important improvements in terms of a more automatic, objective, and continuous monitoring and assessment. Moreover, the latest Explainable AI (XAI) methodologies may make AI decisions interpretable and trustworthy for end users. This paper presents a novel AI framework for early and explainable malnutrition risk detection based on heterogeneous m-health data. We performed an extensive model evaluation including both subject-independent and personalised predictions, and the obtained results indicate Random Forest (RF) and Gradient Boosting as the best performing classifiers, especially when incorporating body composition assessment data. We also investigated several benchmark XAI methods to extract global model explanations. Model-specific explanation consistency assessment indicates that each selected model privileges similar subsets of the most relevant predictors, with the highest agreement shown between SHapley Additive ExPlanations (SHAP) and feature permutation method. Furthermore, we performed a preliminary clinical validation to verify that the learned feature-output trends are compliant with the current evidence-based assessment.
Methods: Longitudinal study in an Italian long-term care facility using the DoEatWell m-health app across 5 trial periods. Compared subject-independent hold-out and Leave-One-Subject-Out CV on clinical, nutritional, and body composition data with ML classifiers and SHAP/LIME/permutation explainability.
Results: Random Forest and gradient boosting were the best classifiers, with hold-out accuracy/F-score above 90% and personalized accuracy around 75%-80% median. SHAP and feature permutation showed largely consistent feature rankings, with BMI or MMSE usually the top predictor, and explanations aligned with clinical evidence.
Conclusions: The framework provided accurate and clinically sound early malnutrition risk prediction, and the best models relied on a consistent subset of predictors. Limitations include variable subject monitoring, failure cases in personalized prediction, and the need for more data and additional variables for stronger generalization.

Source: Initial Diagnosis of Stroke Based on SMOTE- ENN and Hybrid Machine Learning
Abstract: In this paper, a stroke screening model based on SMOTE-ENN and hybrid machine learning is constructed. In view of the imbalance of medical data categories and the fact that the cost of missed diagnosis is significantly higher than that of misdiagnosis in the primary screening scene of stroke, this study constructs a multi-dimensional optimization framework: in the data layer, firstly, the quality of the data set is improved by preprocessing technology, and secondly, SMOTE-ENN is used to balance the data distribution; then, in the model layer, the integration strategies of Bagging, Boosting, Stacking and Voting are integrated. At the same time, a cost-sensitive learning mechanism is embedded in the parameter layer; implement a dynamic threshold optimization strategy at the decision-making layer. Experiments show that Soft Voting (RF: LightGBM: XGBoost = 2: 3: 1) performs best: while maintaining a high accuracy (70.67 %), the false negative rate is reduced to 2.92 % (sensitivity is as high as 97.08 %), the false positive rate is controlled at 29.86 %, and the AUC is 0.836. The balance characteristics of the model ' very low false negative rate-moderate false positive rate ' make it especially suitable for primary screening in primary medical institutions and family health monitoring scenarios, providing reliable technical support for early warning of stroke.
Methods: Stroke screening model using SMOTE-ENN data balancing and hybrid machine learning with Bagging, Boosting, Stacking, and Voting. A cost-sensitive learning mechanism and dynamic threshold optimization were added; Soft Voting combined RF, LightGBM, and XGBoost in a 2:3:1 ratio.
Results: Soft Voting performed best with 70.67% accuracy, 2.92% false negative rate, 97.08% sensitivity, 29.86% false positive rate, and AUC 0.836.
Conclusions: The model is suitable for primary stroke screening because it achieves very low false negatives with moderate false positives. It is intended to support early warning in primary care and family health monitoring.

Journal: Proceedings - 2025 8th International Seminar on Research of Information Technology and Intelligent Systems, ISRITI 2025
Publisher: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers Inc.
Source: Imbalanced Data Handling for Stroke Prediction Using Oversampling and Cost-Sensitive Learning
Abstract: Class imbalance is a major challenge in medical predictive modeling, especially in stroke risk identification, where minority cases represent only a small fraction of the available clinical data. This study compares the effectiveness of two imbalance handling techniques, SMOTE oversampling and cost-sensitive learning, applied to Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and XGBoost using the public Kaggle stroke dataset. Three experimental scenarios were evaluated: baseline, SMOTE, and cost-sensitive learning. The results show a significant improvement in minority class recall, especially for SVM, although this improvement is accompanied by a decrease in overall precision and accuracy. Evaluation using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC shows that cost-sensitive learning provides the best balance between sensitivity and discrimination performance. Further SHAP analysis revealed that age and hypertension were the most influential predictors. Although these findings are promising, limitations related to dataset size and the risk of overfitting remain. Further research should explore hybrid imbalance handling methods and validation on larger and more diverse datasets to improve clinical applicability.
Methods: Comparative experiment on the public Kaggle stroke dataset using Random Forest, SVM, and XGBoost under three scenarios: baseline, SMOTE oversampling, and cost-sensitive learning. Performance was evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC; SHAP was used for feature analysis.
Results: Both imbalance methods improved minority class recall, especially for SVM, but reduced overall precision and accuracy. Cost-sensitive learning gave the best balance of sensitivity and discrimination; age and hypertension were the most influential predictors.
Conclusions: Cost-sensitive learning appears most effective for stroke prediction with imbalanced data. Limitations include dataset size and overfitting risk, and the authors recommend hybrid methods and validation on larger, more diverse datasets.

Journal: International Journal of Optimization and Control: Theories and Applications
Source: Resampling strategies for machine learning-based effort overrun risk detection: A controlled factorial study with cost-sensitive evaluation
Abstract: The Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) has become the default preprocessing step for handling class imbalance in software effort-risk prediction, yet its effectiveness in this domain has not been rigorously tested. This study addresses that gap through a controlled factorial experiment on the publicly available Software Development Effort Dataset Annotated with Expert Estimates dataset, comprising 4,329 software issues from Apache projects drawn from an initial repository of 23,186 records. Six resampling strategies are compared across four classifier families under both standard and cost-sensitive evaluation metrics that weight missed high-risk issues more heavily than false alarms. A secondary contribution is the analysis of how resampling interacts with the extreme class imbalance characteristic of real-world effort data (2.2% minority rate), a regime substantially more severe than those examined in prior investigations. Results are interpreted through SHAP-based feature attribution to determine whether oversampling alters which features the models rely on. The findings reveal two overarching results: near-perfect performance under a full feature set is largely attributable to target leakage rather than a genuine predictive signal, and, under deployment, valid early-warning features degrade cost-sensitive performance relative to no resampling when SMOTE is used. Cost-sensitive weighting emerges as the more reliable alternative, preserving both performance and feature attribution structure. These findings challenge the uncritical adoption of SMOTE in software analytics and carry direct implications for the design of reproducible, interpretable risk-detection pipelines.
Methods: Controlled factorial experiment on the Software Development Effort Dataset Annotated with Expert Estimates (4,329 issues from Apache projects). Six resampling strategies were compared across four classifier families using standard and cost-sensitive evaluation, with SHAP-based feature attribution.
Results: Near-perfect performance with the full feature set was largely due to target leakage, not genuine predictive signal. Under deployment, SMOTE reduced cost-sensitive performance relative to no resampling, while cost-sensitive weighting performed more reliably and preserved feature-attribution structure.
Conclusions: The study challenges uncritical use of SMOTE for software effort-risk detection and supports cost-sensitive weighting as a better alternative. A key limitation is that apparent high performance can reflect leakage rather than true predictive validity.

Authors: Farrow, L.; Anderson, L.; Zhong, M.
Source: Managing class imbalance in the training of a large language model to predict patient selection for total knee arthroplasty: Results from the Artificial intelligence to Revolutionise the patient Care pathway in Hip and knEe aRthroplastY (ARCHERY) project
Abstract: Introduction: This study set out to test the efficacy of different techniques used to manage to class imbalance, a type of data bias, in application of a large language model (LLM) to predict patient selection for total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Methods: This study utilised data from the Artificial Intelligence to Revolutionise the Patient Care Pathway in Hip and Knee Arthroplasty (ARCHERY) project (ISRCTN18398037). Data included the pre-operative radiology reports of patients referred to secondary care for knee-related complaints from within the North of Scotland. A clinically based LLM (GatorTron) was trained regarding prediction of selection for TKA. Three methods for managing class imbalance were assessed: a standard model, use of class weighting, and majority class undersampling. Results: A total of 7707 individual knee radiology reports were included (dated from 2015 to 2022). The mean text length was 74 words (range 26–275). Only 910/7707 (11.8%) patients underwent TKA surgery (the designated ‘minority class’). Class weighting technique performed better for minority class discrimination and calibration compared with the other two techniques (Recall 0.61/AUROC 0.73 for class weighting compared with 0.54/0.70 and 0.59/0.72 for the standard model and majority class undersampling, respectively. There was also significant data loss for majority class undersampling when compared with class-weighting. Conclusion: Use of class-weighting appears to provide the optimal method of training a an LLM to perform analytical tasks on free-text clinical information in the face of significant data bias (‘class imbalance’). Such knowledge is an important consideration in the development of high-performance clinical AI models within Trauma and Orthopaedics.
Methods: Retrospective cohort study using 7,707 knee radiology reports from the ARCHERY project in North of Scotland patients; GatorTron was fine-tuned with stratified 3-fold cross-validation to predict TKA selection. Three class-imbalance strategies were compared: standard training, class weighting, and majority-class undersampling.
Results: Only 910/7,707 patients (11.8%) underwent TKA. Class weighting performed best for minority-class discrimination and calibration, with recall 0.61 and AUROC 0.73 versus 0.54/0.70 for the standard model and 0.59/0.72 for undersampling.
Conclusions: Class weighting was the best approach for handling class imbalance in this LLM task and may improve AI performance in clinical free-text analysis. A key limitation is that the approach was tested in one orthopaedic setting, and other imbalance methods were not evaluated.

Journal: Fundamentals and Methods of Machine and Deep Learning: Algorithms, Tools, and Applications
Source: Application of machine learning algorithms with balancing techniques for credit card fraud detection: A comparative analysis
Abstract: This paper investigates the performance of the four supervised machine learning algorithms: logistic regression, support vector machine, decision tree, and random forest on the highly imbalanced ULB machine learning credit card fraudulent transaction dataset and a comparative analysis is performed. The major point that distinguishes this study from others is that this work is not only focused on the four supervised machine learning algorithms, rather than the permutation and combination of these methods with different balancing techniques are studied and analyzed for several evaluation metrics to obtain a better performance. In addition of the sampling techniques, one more method is used to balance the dataset by taking in account the balanced class weight at the modeling time. It is important to mention that the random forest with balanced class weight has shown the lowest false positive transactions with a value of only 3. The comparative results demonstrate that the random forest with SMOTE oversampling technique has output the best results in terms of all the selected metrics with accuracy of 99.92%, recall value of 81.08%, precision of 76.43%, F1-score of 78.69%, MCC of 0.79, AUC of 0.96, and AUPRC of 0.81.
Methods: Comparative analysis of four supervised models—logistic regression, support vector machine, decision tree, and random forest—on the imbalanced ULB credit card fraud dataset. Models were combined with balancing techniques including sampling methods, SMOTE, and balanced class weights, and evaluated across multiple metrics.
Results: Random forest with SMOTE performed best, achieving 99.92% accuracy, 81.08% recall, 76.43% precision, 78.69% F1-score, 0.79 MCC, 0.96 AUC, and 0.81 AUPRC. Random forest with balanced class weight produced the fewest false positives, with 3.
Conclusions: Random forest with SMOTE was the best-performing approach for credit card fraud detection on this dataset. The study indicates balancing techniques improve performance, with balanced class weights reducing false positives.

Journal: Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Artificial Intelligence
Source: Learning from unbalanced catastrophic out-of-pocket health expenditure dataset: blending SMOTE-boosting with ensemble models
Abstract: This study attests to the benefits of synthetic data generation with the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE), and it incorporates this procedure with SMOTEBoosting by applying learning algorithms to model unbalanced catastrophic out-of-pocket (OOP) health expenditure dataset. Nationally representative household budget survey data were gathered from Turkish Statistical Institute for the year 2012. A total of 9987 households responded to the survey. The original dataset was highly unbalanced and a total of 0.14% of households faced catastrophic health expenses. SMOTE was used to perform balanced oversampling, and 10 artificial datasets with sizes from 10% to 100% of the majority group of original training data were generated. To predict OOP catastrophic health expenditures, the SMOTEBoosting was embedded with learning algorithms, such as C5.0, random forest (RF), naïve Bayes, and support vector machine. Study results confirm the outstanding prediction performance of the blended strategy of SMOTEBoosting with RF (area under the curve ˃ 0.85) for prediction. A variable importance plot and decision tree visualise that at least 65 years of age is the most important predictor of the catastrophic cases. The findings of this study highlight that multistrategy ensemble learning techniques are useful to model highly unbalanced datasets.
Methods: Nationally representative Turkish household budget survey data from 2012 were analyzed (n=9,987 households). SMOTE-generated balanced datasets (10 artificial sets, 10%-100% of the majority group) were combined with SMOTEBoosting and classifiers including C5.0, random forest, naïve Bayes, and support vector machine.
Results: The blended SMOTEBoosting + random forest approach achieved outstanding prediction performance (AUC > 0.85). At least 65 years of age was the most important predictor of catastrophic cases.
Conclusions: Multistrategy ensemble learning techniques are useful for modeling highly unbalanced catastrophic health expenditure datasets.
